h1: 24 Car Logos That Look Way Too Similar

contentBlocks.text: Have you ever looked at a car and realized you have no idea what brand it actually is until you get right up close to it?

Car companies spend a massive amount of money on branding, often hiring expensive agencies to come up with logos that are supposed to be completely unique. They usually release these long explanations about how a specific curve represents the spirit of driving or some other vague concept.

But when you actually see these badges on the street, it feels like everyone is working from the same template. Some of these designs are so similar it’s hard to believe they were created independently. You’ll find high-end European brands that look almost exactly like budget cars from the other side of the world, or luxury SUVs that seem to have borrowed their entire aesthetic from a brand you’ve never heard of.
It makes you wonder if it’s just a coincidence or if some designers are just looking at what everyone else is doing and making minor tweaks.
I found 12 pairs of car logos that are so close to each other they’ll probably make you look twice. Let's get into the ones that stand out the most.
1. Lamborghini vs. Arash - Similarity: 85%
2. Rover vs. Roewe - Similarity: 80%
3. Bugatti vs. Diatto - Similarity: 75%
4. Bentley vs. JBA Motors - Similarity: 70%
5. Ford vs. Karry - Similarity: 70%
6. BMW vs. BYD - Similarity: 67%
7. Mercedes-Benz vs. SANY - Similarity: 65%
8. Oldsmobile vs. Mahindra - Similarity: 58%
9. Kia vs. BYD - Similarity: 50%
10. Infiniti vs. Chery - Similarity: 48%
11. Acura vs. Changan - Similarity: 38%
12. Mazda vs. Haima - Similarity: 30%
1. Lamborghini vs. Arash
Similarity: 85%
Honestly, if this thing flashed past you on the highway, you’d swear you just saw a Lamborghini.

Arash is this tiny British supercar company that basically looked at Lambo's logo and said, "Yeah, we'll take that." They didn't just get inspired; they straight-up copied the whole vibe. You get the exact same gold-on-black colors and the identical sharp, upside-down triangle shield.
The only reason they probably didn't get sued into oblivion is that they swapped out Lamborghini's famous raging bull for an eagle.
It takes some serious guts to copy one of the most recognizable brands on the planet, but hey, if you want people to think your car is fast, I guess you might as well look like a Lambo.
2. Rover vs. Roewe
Similarity: 80%
This one is actually a legendary piece of automotive drama.

Roewe is a brand owned by the Chinese auto giant SAIC, and their cars were originally built using technology bought from the defunct British carmaker MG Rover. SAIC wanted to buy the actual "Rover" name too, but the deal fell through. Since they couldn't use the real name, they did the next best thing—they invented a new brand that sounds almost identical.
But they didn't stop at the name. They also copied the whole look of the classic Rover badge, using the exact same shield shape and red-and-gold color scheme.

It’s basically the automotive equivalent of buying a knockoff brand called "Mike" that uses a checkmark logo. It’s a clever legal loophole, but anyone who knows cars can see exactly what they did there.
3. Bugatti vs. Diatto
Similarity: 75%

If you look at the Bugatti badge, you see one of the most famous and expensive logos in automotive history. But if you look at the logo for Diatto—a classic Italian brand that stopped making cars back in the 1920s—you might think you are experiencing double vision.
Both logos feature a prominent red oval with a thick white border, lined with tiny red dots, and the brand name written in bold block letters across the center.

The similarity actually makes a lot of sense when you look at the history. Both companies were started by Italians around the same era, and Ettore Bugatti himself actually worked with Diatto early in his career, even helping them design some race cars.
So while it looks like a total copy job at first glance, this is probably just a case of two old-school European creators sharing the exact same design language during the birth of the sports car.
4. Bentley vs. JBA Motors
Similarity: 70%
Using wings on a car logo is a common way to make a brand look fast and high-end. Bentley is probably the most famous example of this with its Flying B badge.

However, JBA Motors, a small British company that makes retro-style roadsters, uses a design that is almost identical. Both logos have two detailed wings spreading out from a central oval that shows the company's first letter. Bentley uses a B, while JBA uses a J.
Since JBA builds cars that look like they are from the 1930s, they might have just wanted to match that vintage British luxury style.
But considering Bentley had been using those wings for decades before JBA even started in the 1980s, it seems pretty clear that they were heavily inspired by the Bentley design.
5. Ford vs. Karry
Similarity: 70%

The classic Ford oval is one of the most sacred logos in the entire automotive world. So, when Chery launched its commercial brand, Karry, back in the late 2000s, people immediately did a double-take.

It wasn't just a slight resemblance; they basically copied the entire setup. Both badges have the exact same look: a horizontal oval, a deep blue background, a thin white border line, and white flowing script running right through the middle.
The only real giveaway that you aren't looking at a regular Ford van is that the cursive letters spell out "Karry" instead of "Ford."

Putting white cursive text inside a blue oval is an old loophole that keeps budget brands out of legal trouble. But when your logo forces people to squint just to make sure they aren't looking at a Ford, it’s pretty obvious where you got the idea.
6. BMW vs. BYD
Similarity: 67%
Long before BYD was everywhere on the global EV market, they started out with a logo that definitely made car enthusiasts do a double-take.

Back in the early 2000s, their first badge looked an awful lot like BMW’s classic roundel. Both designs shared the exact same visual recipe: blue and white quarters inside a circle, wrapped in a thick black ring. The only real twist was that BYD flattened the shape into an oval and swapped the iconic German letters for their own initials.
It was a pretty common move for a brand-new automaker at the time—using a familiar, premium look to help people get comfortable with a new name on the road.

Thankfully, BYD has completely moved on and found a modern style that's 100% their own. Still, looking back at that vintage oval is a great reminder of just how much the company has changed over the years.
7. Mercedes-Benz vs. SANY
Similarity: 65%
If you see a SANY cement mixer or excavator rumbling down a construction site, it’s hard not to wonder if Mercedes-Benz secretly started a heavy machinery division.

The German luxury icon is famous for its elegant three-pointed star, which originally stood for dominating land, sea, and air. SANY, the Chinese heavy equipment giant, uses three interlocking diamond points inside a circle. Their official corporate story is that "SANY" means "Three Ones," representing their goals of building a top-tier company, hiring top talent, and making a real contribution to society.

Mercedes' parent company, Daimler, wasn't about to just let that slide. They launched a brutal, multi-front trademark war, suing SANY at home in China and following them all the way to international markets like the UK and New Zealand, desperate to block the Chinese brand from expanding overseas.

But that global legal siege backfired completely. Courts around the world repeatedly threw out Mercedes' complaints. The judges essentially pointed out the obvious: anyone shopping for a million-dollar industrial crane isn't going to accidentally walk home with a SANY thinking they bought a luxury German sedan. It was a massive victory for SANY, but out on the street, you still can’t look at that three-pronged logo without seeing a Mercedes shadow.
8. Oldsmobile vs. Mahindra
Similarity: 58%
This is one of those cases where two design teams took completely different corporate philosophies and somehow ended up sketching the exact same thing.

The classic Oldsmobile badge is a bit of American car history—it’s an asymmetrical logo showing a rocket ship blasting right through an oval, symbolizing the brand breaking boundaries. But if you looked at the old logo for Mahindra, the Indian manufacturing giant, you’d swear it was a mirror image.
Mahindra’s official story is that their badge is a stylized letter "M" with three divisions pointing upward, representing their corporate branches of products, services, and possibilities.

But out on the street, nobody is thinking about "corporate possibilities." They just see a silver oval with an angled line cutting through it. Even though the meanings are worlds apart, the visual overlap is so close it’s hard not to see the old Oldsmobile spirit every time you look at a Mahindra SUV.
9. Kia vs. BYD
Similarity: 50%
This one is the ultimate corporate default setting. It feels less like somebody copied homework and more like two different companies used the exact same generic Microsoft Word template.

Before both of these brands went through massive, expensive redesigns, Kia and BYD were sharing the exact same highway aesthetic. Both logos were just a basic red oval with a silver border and the company's name slapped right in the middle in plain, capital letters.
The only thing separating a budget Korean sedan from an early Chinese sedan was whether the red badge spelled out "KIA" or "BYD."

Putting your name in a red oval is about as creative as naming your dog "Dog," but it’s a safe, corporate look that gets the job done. Thankfully, both companies eventually realized how boring this was and rolled out the modern, edgy text-based logos we see on the streets today.
10. Infiniti vs. Chery
Similarity: 48%

This pairing is less about a direct clone job and more about a hilarious case of accidental geometry. Corporate-wise, Nissan’s luxury division and the Chinese automaker have absolutely zero relationship, but their latest design choices have left them sharing a very specific punchline.

For years, car geeks cracked jokes about the two brands, but you could always tell them apart because Chery’s old logo had a sharp capital "A" that locked directly into the top of the frame. But when Chery rolled out its new, flattened logo, they detached that inner piece and smoothed it out into a rounded arch floating inside a silver ring.
Now, they look like positive and negative mirrors of each other.

Infiniti’s badge is an oval with a sharp, open "V" pointing upward, symbolizing a highway stretching into the infinite horizon. Chery’s new badge is a distinct circle with a smooth, open arch pointing downward, meant to represent a mountain peak. They aren't going to fool anyone who actually looks at the shape of the outer ring, but the "upside-down mirror" vibe is a fun coincidence that car enthusiasts won’t let either brand live down anytime soon.
11. Acura vs. Changan
Similarity: 38%
This is one of the most famous lookalikes in the car world, and it basically looks like what happens when you take one logo and turn it upside down.

Acura’s badge is a stylized letter "A" designed to look like a pair of engineering calipers, symbolizing precision and quality. On the other hand, Changan uses a sharp "V" shape inside its silver oval, which represents "Victory" and "Value."

Both of those corporate meanings make perfect sense, but the visual contrast between the two logos is hard to ignore. Because the geometric shapes are so clean and similar, car enthusiasts have spent years joking that one logo is just the inverse of the other.

It’s almost certainly a genuine coincidence born from two different design teams trying to fit a sharp, pointy letter inside a standard silver ring. Still, once you notice the upside-down relationship, it’s a fun detail that’s impossible to unsee.
12. Mazda vs. Haima
Similarity: 30%
This one is basically a case of a bad breakup where one person kept the other person’s aesthetic.

For years, Haima was a Chinese car company working in a joint venture with Mazda, building cars based on the Japanese brand’s platforms. But when their partnership officially wrapped up in the late 2000s, Haima didn't exactly throw out the old corporate design manual.

Mazda’s actual logo is that famous, highly-styled letter "M" with its arms stretched out like wings, symbolizing the brand flying toward the future. Haima’s official story for their own badge is that it represents a mythical bird flying away from a rising sun.

Corporate poetry aside, it looks like someone just took the Mazda wings, squeezed them together at the top, and tweaked the frame. It’s a literal graphic design leftover from a former relationship, making it pretty obvious to anyone on the road exactly where Haima got their start.
Conclusion: Synergy, or Just Lazy Design?

At the end of the day, there are only so many geometric shapes you can fit onto the grille of a car. When you mix that limitation with a global industry where everyone is chasing the same premium aesthetic, a few visual overlaps are bound to happen.

Sometimes, it really is just a case of "great minds thinking alike." Two designers on opposite sides of the world can easily sketch a sharp letter inside a silver circle and arrive at the exact same conclusion without ever looking at each other's work.

But other times? It's pretty hard to give the benefit of the doubt. Whether it's a legal loophole to bypass a trademark, a rookie brand trying to borrow some German street cred, or a leftover design from an old corporate partnership, some of these badges are just too close for comfort.
So, what do you think? Are these car companies showcasing brilliant design synergy, or did they just straight-up copy their homework?

We’ve laid out the biggest lookalikes on the road, and while some have a historic excuse, others are just too blatant to ignore. The next time you spot one of these badges speeding down the highway, you’ll know exactly which brand was chasing whose shadow.
